title: HUMAN TERRITORIALITY
review_question: To review and synthesize the existing literature on human territoriality, including its definitions, theoretical frameworks, and empirical evidence, and to identify outstanding issues and future research directions.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly defined, but focuses on psychological and ethological literature concerning human territoriality, drawing comparisons to animal territoriality.

findings.quote: A comparison of definitions of human territoriality demonstrates the variety in interpretations of the human expression.
Theoretical work on human territoriality includes a small number of classificatory systems and conceptualizations, but no comprehensive theory.
No particular paradigm characterizes research on the topic, and as yet there is no standard set of principles that can be reliably applied to problems in the area.

findings.antecedent: Animal territoriality concepts (e.g., Wynne-Edwards, Lorenz, Ardrey)
findings.quote: Part of the appeal of Wynne-Edwards' theory is that it appears to apply to humans too... There are attractive analogs to animal territorial relationships in human society...

findings.antecedent: Gross similarities between animal and human territorial behavior
findings.consequent: Underlying mechanisms being the same (e.g., genetic basis)
findings.quote: Despite Ardrey's arguments, it does not follow from the gross similarities between the territorial behavior of some animals and man that the underlying mechanisms are the same in both, nor that they are genetic.
Human use of space is very variable and not like the stereotypic spatial expressions of animals. This suggests a learned, rather than a genetic, basis.
man, with many vertebrates, often displays a positive correlation between social status in a local community and the size of his territory there.

findings.consequent: Substitution of pecking order (hierarchy) for democratic territorial order
findings.quote: animals will sometimes substitute a pecking order (hierarchy) for a relatively democratic territorial order if crowded to the point that there is no room for individual territories

findings.consequent: Dominance of an individual over others
findings.quote: An individual dominates all others so long as he is on home ground; territory is thus a social equalizer for lower ranking organisms.

findings.consequent: Social order and structure in communities
findings.quote: Territoriality is important as a behavior system that is woven into the social organization of communities.

findings.consequent: Definition and organization of social role relationships
findings.quote: territoriality is instrumental in the definition and organization of various role relationships

findings.consequent: Sense of security and identity for the individual
findings.quote: Ardrey (1966) stated that territory stimulates the individual, and gives a sense of security and identity
A clear benefit provided by many, but not all, territories is privacy (the right of the individual to decide what information about himself should be communicated to others).
In all cases psychological privacy serves to maximize freedom of choice
crowding occurs when 'the number of people an individual is in contact with is sufficient to prevent him from carrying out some specific behavior and thereby restricts his freedom of choice'

findings.consequent: Control over space, power, influence, comfort
findings.quote: Territorial behavior, in Roos's scheme, is something that maximizes a person's control over space to enhance its positive value, and territory itself gives the potential for power, influence, comfort, and control
Inmates' seats obviously became more than something to sit in; as territories they had psychic and emotional significance to their occupants.

findings.consequent: Territorial behavior patterns (e.g., top third move freely, bottom third claim remote areas, middle third claim larger central territories)
findings.quote: Generally speaking, the top one third of the dominance hierarchy moved freely over the ward, and defended no personal territories. The bottom one third tended to claim spaces in remote areas of the ward. The middle third claimed larger territories and in central parts of the ward.
these individuals won 85% of all attempted physical acts of dominance on home territory, and 55% of those off home ground.

findings.consequent: Reduction of psychological complexity and enhancement of personal control
findings.quote: Territories were interpreted by the investigators as basic and necessary reducers of psychological complexity in the boys' lives and enhancers of personal control for them
It appeared that 'territorial adaptation' was effective for raising status inside the building, but not for functioning on the outside.
the relationship between territoriality and dominance has received mixed support.
Colman (1968) described striking changes in demeanor and behavior of a medical patient that occurred when the patient moved from a hospital setting to his own home.

findings.consequent: Space per person in claimed territory
findings.quote: Group territories were found not to expand regularly with number of people in the group; instead, space per person tended to decrease as group size increased.
Territory size increased with time in same-sex groups, but mixed groups tended to deploy markers as time passed.

findings.antecedent: Defended homes ('no trespassing' signs and fences)
findings.quote: families living in defended homes had lived significantly longer on the property, but also anticipated a longer residence there in the future.

findings.consequent: Speed of answering the door (defensive vigilance)
findings.quote: occupants of property with 'no trespassing' signs answered the door significantly faster than controls (interpreted as heightened defensive vigilance).
Under heavy demand for space, more personal markers (personal jackets, sweaters) were more effective than impersonal ones.

findings.antecedent: Marked tables (vs. unmarked or clear tables)
findings.quote: given a choice, people prefer to settle at unmarked tables than marked ones; (b) if they do settle at marked tables, people spend less time there than at clear tables.

findings.consequent: Potential invaders spacing themselves from markers
findings.quote: effectiveness of a marker in reserving a space claim occurs not because it signifies an area is occupied, but because potential invaders space themselves from markers as they would from other people

findings.antecedent: Spatial invasion of marked claims in cafeterias
findings.quote: most occupants of cafeteria places (31 out of 33) flee when spatially invaded

findings.antecedent: Stationary groups (high-status vs. low-status; four people vs. two people)
findings.consequent: Passersby walking through the group (boundary permeability)
findings.quote: fewer passersby walked through stationary high-status groups than low-status groups, and fewer through a group of four than a group of two.

findings.consequent: Invasion of space between them by passersby
findings.quote: Beyond four feet (the limit of Hall's, 1966, 'personal distance') the boundary surrounding the stationary pair becomes ineffective, and passersby begin to walk between the conversationalists.

findings.antecedent: Gender of stationary conversing pair (female or male-female vs. male)
findings.quote: intrusion is less frequent when the stationary conversing pair is female, or a male-female combination, than when it is male.

findings.consequent: Emotional effects on invaders (agonistic facial expressions, negative mood)
findings.quote: moving invaders were emotionally affected by the experience, displaying subtle, agonistic facial expressions during the invasion, and giving negative mood ratings immediately afterwards.

findings.antecedent: Prior experience with a physical environment (room)
findings.consequent: Distance subjects stand from a stranger
findings.quote: prior experience with the room reduced the distance subjects would stand from a stranger later introduced into the environment

findings.antecedent: Anticipated future return to an environment
findings.consequent: Claimed floor space (in model building task) when stranger present
findings.quote: subjects claimed more floor space (in a model building task) when the stranger was present if they anticipated future return to the environment.

findings.antecedent: Architectural features (e.g., number of floors, corridor arrangement)
findings.quote: Newman (1972) pointed out specific architectural features in some apartment buildings that promote alienation among tenants

findings.antecedent: Architectural features (e.g., promoting common territory defense)
findings.consequent: Cohesion among building occupants and defense against antisocial behavior
findings.quote: recommendations for future designs that will promote both cohesion among building occupants and defense of common territory in and around buildings, reducing antisocial behavior there.

synthesis_conclusions: Human territoriality is a complex, multifaceted phenomenon linking behavior to geographic places, with diverse definitions and theoretical approaches.
While animal analogies are attractive, human territoriality differs significantly, being more variable, learned, and serving secondary purposes beyond basic biological needs.
Territoriality is empirically related to social status, control, identity, privacy, and social order, with evidence from institutional, public, and experimental settings.
The field is in a pre-paradigmatic stage, characterized by fragmented research and a lack of comprehensive theory, but is expanding and relevant to environmental issues.
Key psychological benefits of territory include security, identity, freedom of action, and privacy, which in turn maximizes freedom of choice and reduces crowding.
evidence_gaps: Whether territorial expression operates hydraulically (expression in one mode reduces another) or snowballing (more one gets, more one wants).
Whether territory is necessary for health, happiness, and efficient functioning in humans.
Whether fulfillment of related needs (privacy, status, ownership) can satisfy a 'territory drive'.
The specific determinants of territorial behavior, especially the role of genetics.
The meaningful application of territoriality to cognitive domains (e.g., defending ideas, opinions, creative products).
Whether territoriality is always beneficial, or if there are detrimental conditions (e.g., reinforcing social status distinctions, promoting chauvinism).
The extent to which legal decisions involving territory align with psychological knowledge.
The existence and characteristics of territorial 'personalities'.
Research on individual and group territoriality, relationships to social organization, sex differences, developmental aspects, and cultural differences.
Clarification of the concept's relationship to adjacent concepts like privacy, interpersonal distance, and jurisdiction.

moderators.effect: Retardates prefer filled territorial spaces, while normals prefer open spaces and are less aggressive.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Retardates prefer filled spaces; normals prefer open spaces and are less aggressive.

moderators.effect: At moderate density, most objects protect space; under heavy demand, personal markers are more effective.
Longer absence reduces neighbor support for a marked claim.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Social support for claims diminishes with time.

moderators.variable: Group status and size (of obstructing group)
moderators.effect: Fewer passersby walk through high-status or larger groups.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Boundary permeability is affected by group status and size.

moderators.effect: Intrusion is less frequent for female or male-female pairs compared to male pairs.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Boundary permeability is affected by gender composition.

moderators.effect: Territoriality is accelerated in pairs with incompatible traits during social isolation.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Spatial adaptation to stressful conditions is partly a function of personality.

limitations: Many forms of territoriality are difficult to study in standard laboratory settings due to long association periods and difficulty eliciting personal attachment.
Generalizing from institutionalized samples may be hazardous due to unusual subjects and settings.
The research literature sometimes appears disjointed due to a variety of operational definitions and methodologies.
The field is still in a pre-paradigmatic stage with loose ideas and definitional problems.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Human territoriality is a multi-faceted, dynamic system involving primary, secondary, and public territories, serving functions like identity, security, and control, and is expressed through various behaviors and markers.
While acknowledging animal territoriality, human territoriality is more complex, involving symbolic, cultural, and social dimensions beyond mere physical defense of space.
Individuals strive to achieve an optimal level of privacy, and territoriality is one mechanism to regulate social interaction and achieve desired privacy levels.

mechanism_chain.description: A proposed mechanism for how territoriality functions to regulate social interaction and achieve desired privacy.

steps.from_construct: Need for privacy/control over social interaction
steps.to_construct: Use of territorial markers (e.g., personal items, fences, verbal claims)
Communication of ownership/exclusive access to others
Regulation of social interaction and reduced intrusion
